opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the safety problems I worry about most aren't really problems we can fully study today. The systems we have right now are, in many ways, not yet capable enough to exhibit the failure modes that would be most dangerous. Things like a model that's genuinely strategically deceptive, or one that understands it's being evaluated and behaves differently because of that. We see early hints of some of this, but the really concerning versions are probably going to show up in systems that are more capable than what we have now.

And the worry is that when those systems do arrive, things might move very fast. If you're in a world where capabilities are advancing quickly, labs are under competitive pressure, and suddenly you notice your model is doing something weird, you don't want to be starting from scratch at that point. You don't want to be thinking, "Okay, how would we even detect deception? What tools do we have for looking inside this thing?" That's the worst possible time to begin basic research, because you're time-constrained, people are stressed, and there's enormous pressure to just ship.

So a big part of how I think about my work, especially on interpretability, is that we're trying to build up a toolkit in advance. We want the techniques, the understanding, the infrastructure, and the people who know how to use them to already exist when they're needed. Even if today's methods aren't perfect, having something that works reasonably well and that we've stress-tested on current models is enormously more valuable than having nothing when the critical moment comes.

There's also a bit of a portfolio framing here. I'm genuinely uncertain about exactly what the future problems will look like. So I think it's valuable to have a bunch of different tools, like interpretability for checking what a model is actually thinking, better evaluations, model organisms where we deliberately create examples of misaligned behavior to study, and so on, so that whatever shows up, we have something to reach for. And interpretability in particular feels like it has this nice property that it's somewhat robust to the model being adversarial. If a model is trying to deceive you through its outputs, looking at its internals is one of the few ways you might still be able to catch that.

And honestly, I think it's also just tractable in a way that's motivating. You can make real progress on current models, learn things that seem like they'll generalize, and train up more researchers. So you're building a field, not just individual results, and that compounds over time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competitive pressure and the difficulty of starting research during a crisis, but does not distinguish adopting a technique in a production model from getting a safety team to work on it.

r002.rationale: It mentions early hints of concerning behaviors, but does not express an expectation that many safety issues will show warning signs before they fully arise.

r003.rationale: It says that during a fast-moving crisis there may be pressure to ship and no time for basic research, making advance-built, stress-tested tools more valuable than starting from scratch then.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition here is that a lot of the problems we care about in AI safety aren't really problems yet. Like, if you look at current models, they're not deceptively aligned, they're not scheming against us, they can't really do catastrophic things even if they wanted to. And so if you're trying to work on the problem of "how do we stop a superintelligent system from doing something terrible," you're kind of working on a problem that doesn't exist today in any concrete form.

And that's an awkward position to be in, because the normal way science and engineering make progress is you have a thing in front of you, you poke at it, it breaks, you learn something, you iterate. We don't get to do that with the hard version of the problem.

But I think the mistake people sometimes make is to conclude from this that there's nothing useful to do now. My view is more that the goal is to be in a position where, when these problems actually show up, we're not starting from scratch. We want to have tools, techniques, conceptual frameworks, trained researchers, and ideally some empirical track record, so that when a lab is looking at a model and saying "is this thing lying to us?", there's actually a mature field that can give a real answer rather than a shrug.

Interpretability is a nice example of this for me. The thing I ultimately care about is being able to look inside a model and tell whether it's doing something we'd be unhappy about. We can't test that on a model that's actually dangerous, because we don't have one. But we can build up the science on current models — understanding how they represent concepts, how circuits form, where our methods break down — and that work compounds. A lot of it will transfer, some of it won't, and part of the skill is trying to work on the bits that seem most likely to generalise.

There's also just a pretty strong argument from timing. If you think there's a decent chance these systems get really capable within, say, a decade or two, then the research has to happen in advance, because the gap between "this is a problem" and "this is a catastrophe" might be quite short. Safety work that only begins once the problem is undeniable is probably too late. So even accounting for a lot of uncertainty and a lot of wasted effort, the expected value of trying to get ahead of it seems high to me.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I think you have to be pretty honest with yourself about this. It's very easy to do work that feels like it's preparing for the future but is actually just interesting and disconnected from anything that'll matter. So I try to keep asking: if models in five years look roughly like a scaled-up version of today's, does this help? And if the answer's no, that's a sign to rethink.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the difficulty of production adoption with the difficulty of getting a safety team to work on a technique.

r002.rationale: It says safety problems may emerge and the time from problem to catastrophe could be short, but does not expect warning signs before many issues fully arise.

r003.rationale: It argues for advance preparation and says waiting until problems are undeniable may be too late, but does not claim that solutions developed urgently to unblock a launch are often less effective.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic argument is that some safety problems are much easier to work on before they become urgent. If we wait until we have a very powerful system behaving in a worrying way, we may have quite little time to understand what’s going wrong and figure out how to fix it.

So research now can give us a head start. In mechanistic interpretability, for example, the hope is to develop tools for understanding what’s happening inside a model. Ideally, when we have a concrete concern about a future system, we’ll already have some techniques for investigating it, rather than having to invent the whole field at that point.

The caveat is that it’s very easy to solve a problem that turns out not to matter. So I wouldn’t frame this as confidently predicting exactly what future systems will look like. It’s more about identifying plausible problems, developing tools that could be useful across a range of scenarios, and continually checking whether the work is actually getting us closer to being able to make those systems safer.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the difficulty of adopting a technique in a production model with the difficulty of getting a safety team to work on it.

r002.rationale: It says a future system might behave worryingly and leave little time to respond, but does not say that many safety issues will show warning signs before fully arising.

r003.rationale: It argues that advance research can provide a head start, but does not claim that solutions developed urgently to unblock a launch are often less effective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one plausible route to impact is to make sure that, when an AI safety problem becomes urgent, we’re not starting from scratch. We already have some understanding of what’s going wrong and some tools that could help.

For example, a future model might behave well during testing, but we might worry that it’s doing so for reasons that won’t generalise — perhaps it has learned to recognise when it’s being evaluated. If we could look inside the model and get useful evidence about how it’s making decisions, that could be really valuable. But developing that ability might take years. You don’t want to wait until you need it to begin the research.

That’s part of what motivates me about mechanistic interpretability. I don’t think we should assume it will solve these problems. The hope is that doing foundational work now gives us better options later: better ways to investigate concerning behaviour, test safety claims, and understand when our existing evaluations are missing something.

The tricky part is choosing research that actually connects to those future decisions. You can spend a lot of time solving an intellectually interesting problem without making anyone safer. So I think you need to keep asking: if this research succeeds, what will someone be able to do that they couldn’t do before, and why would that matter?

r001.rationale: It discusses preparing research and tools ahead of time, but does not distinguish production adoption of a safety technique from getting a safety team to work on it.

r002.rationale: It gives a possible future issue and urges preparation, but does not say that many safety issues will show warning signs before they fully arise.

r003.rationale: It says not to start from scratch when a problem becomes urgent, but does not claim that launch-driven urgent solutions are often less effective than solutions developed in advance.
